content.text:
# Case Study: Anonymous regional fleet

## October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted

*Sector: read from your inputs as logistics tech. Business model: not stated. Tell us how you charge and the plan will adjust.*

*Built from: challenge: given; solution: given; results: 1 item; customer quote: not given; industry: not given.*

Use not approved. The supplied permission statement does not authorise publication. Keep this draft internal until the customer approves the wording, attribution and channels.

---

## The Story (draft)

**The situation.** Anonymous regional fleet is in the logistics tech segment. (General note for logistics tech, not from your inputs: teams are usually judged on on time delivery and cost per shipment or per order.)

**The challenge.** Before Dispatch planning software, the team was dealing with this, in your words: daily route adjustments took four hours.

**The approach.** The team put Dispatch planning software in place: give each depot a shared exception queue.

**The result.** October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted.

**To add before this is published:** (1) one line Anonymous regional fleet would say aloud about what changed, approved in writing.

*The sections below hold the detail behind each part of the story and the questions that finish it.*

---

### About Anonymous regional fleet

| Detail | Supplied information |
|---|---|
| **Customer** | Anonymous regional fleet |
| **Industry** | not given (add customer industry) |
| **Product** | Dispatch planning software |
| **Lead result** | October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted. |

---

## The Challenge

What the team was dealing with: Daily route adjustments took four hours

**Before publication, the account owner should confirm with the customer:**
- What the problem cost them, with the starting value of one of: on time delivery, cost per shipment or per order and order cycle time.
- Interview question in the sector's language: "Which systems hold your orders, shipments and stock today, and who owns the data in them?"

---

## The Solution

What was put in place: Give each depot a shared exception queue

**Before publication, the account owner should verify:**
- Why Anonymous regional fleet chose Dispatch planning software, and which alternative it weighed (a common reaction in logistics tech: "We already have a system for this").
- How the implementation went, and how long it took to see value. Use only a duration the customer confirms.
- Words to use as the customer says them: shipment, carrier, consignment, lead time, exception.

---

## The Results

**Outcomes**

- October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted.

**Before publication, the evidence owner should check each figure:** record the value before, the value after and the measurement period. A strong proof point here: A before and after of on time delivery or cost per shipment on one lane, site or region, measured over a full cycle of busy and quiet weeks.

---

## In Their Words

No customer quote was given. Ask for one line the customer would say aloud about what changed in on time delivery, and get written approval before you print it.

---

## Where This Goes Next

Before changing your process, record the starting point for Dispatch planning software in one comparable case. Agree the measure and review period with the person who owns the work, then compare the result before extending the change.

---

## Sector Notes: Logistics tech

- **A strong proof point here:** A before and after of on time delivery or cost per shipment on one lane, site or region, measured over a full cycle of busy and quiet weeks.
- **What readers in this sector measure:** on time delivery, cost per shipment or per order, order cycle time, exception rate, delay and damage claims, service level attainment, manual planning time.
- **Terms this sector's buyers use:** shipment, carrier, consignment, lead time, exception, service level, proof of delivery, third party logistics provider, transport management system, warehouse management system.
- **Your results:** they carry a figure.

---

## Distribution Formats

Distribution held. Obtain written approval for the exact wording, attribution and intended channels before drafting public versions.
---

## Check Before You Publish

- The customer has approved the story, every figure and the quote in writing.
- Every figure comes from the customer or a page you can cite; page claims stay labelled as the vendor's own claims.
- Nothing in the recognition or company-wide claims is shown as this customer's result.



## Reading the answer

This story supports a draft account of “October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted”. Source verification and written permission for the exact wording remain separate checks. A single pilot is not proof of general or causal improvement. Keep the stated hold in place; this guidance does not override it. The conclusion needs review if the original records alter the baseline, measurement period or sample, or the customer declines the proposed wording or use.

## Decisions by role

Proposed owners. Confirm the named person before acting. Supplied statements below are inputs to check, not established findings.

Founder: ask the evidence owner to distinguish observation from attribution in “October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted”; endorse only the supported scope.

CEO: ask the publication owner for written customer approval of “October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted” and the intended channels; keep distribution on hold until it is recorded.

CMO: compare “Daily route adjustments took four hours” and “October pilot: route adjustment time fell from four to three hours across ten dispatch days. Customer publication permission has not been granted” with the original records; retain sample and period in the final story before requesting approval.

CRO: ask the account owner whether “Give each depot a shared exception queue” explains the buyer's next decision; do not promise another account the same outcome.

Demand generation head: test a reader action to measure the starting point for “Dispatch planning software”; check the destination and permission before distributing the story.

Name one owner per urgent alert. Separate false positives from delayed responses. No measured improvement has been established.

content.text:
# Webinar Script: Reduce invoice exceptions before the payment run

---

## Exercise preparation
Example needed before delivery: supply one anonymised case, its starting records and the decision participants should make. No exercise result is invented. State it as an Example line in the existing takeaway notes.

## Key Takeaways for Audience

1. You will learn how to count exceptions.
2. You will learn how to name an approval owner.
3. You will learn how to compare cycle time before and after one batch.

---

## Run of Show

| Time | Duration | Section | Purpose |
|------|----------|---------|----------|
| 0:00 | 3 min | Welcome & Housekeeping | Set expectations |
| 0:03 | 2 min | Speaker Introduction | Build credibility |
| 0:05 | 2 min | Agenda & Learning Objectives | Preview value |
| 0:07 | 5 min | Context Setting | Why this matters now |
| 0:12 | 12 min | Main Content Block 1 | Core teaching |
| 0:24 | 12 min | Main Content Block 2 | Core teaching |
| 0:36 | 10 min | Main Content Block 3 | Core teaching |
| 0:46 | 4 min | Summary & Key Takeaways | Reinforce learning |
| 0:50 | 8 min | Q&A | Address questions |
| 0:58 | 2 min | Close & CTA | Next steps |

---

## Full Script

### Welcome & Housekeeping (3 min)

**ON SCREEN: Title slide with the webinar name**

**SPEAKER:**
"Welcome to today's session on 'Reduce invoice exceptions before the payment run' with Invoice processing service. This session runs 60 minutes and is for accounts payable heads at regional insurers.

Put your questions in the chat at any time; we have set time aside for them near the end. We will run polls along the way, so keep the poll window open."

### Speaker Introduction (2 min)

**ON SCREEN: Speaker slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"I am your host for this session, from Invoice processing service. Over the next 60 minutes we will look at the problem, the evidence on record and what to do first."

### Agenda & Learning Objectives (2 min)

**ON SCREEN: Agenda slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"Here is how we will use the time. Part one covers Count exceptions. Part two covers how to name an approval owner. Part three covers how to compare cycle time before and after one batch.

By the end of this session, you should be able to say where you stand on approval cycle time and what to change first."

### Context Setting (5 min)

**ON SCREEN: Context slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"Our topic today is 'Reduce invoice exceptions before the payment run'.

For accounts payable heads at regional insurers, the usual yardsticks are approval cycle time and payment success rate.

Among regional insurers, the people who decide this are usually Chief Financial Officer, Finance Controller and Head of Accounts Payable."

**LAUNCH POLL: "Which of these is closest to your situation today?"**
Poll options:
- We measure approval cycle time today and know where we stand
- We know approval cycle time matters but do not measure it yet
- Migration will disrupt the close: that is what holds us back
- This is not a priority this year

### Main Content Block 1 (12 min)

**HOST PREPARATION, NOT SPOKEN:** This exercise needs an anonymised example and its starting records before delivery. Ask the host to supply them; no customer result is assumed.

The reserved 12 minutes cover the example, one participant decision record and a debrief on evidence and unknowns. Do not run this section until the example is ready.

### Main Content Block 2 (12 min)

**ON SCREEN: Key concept slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"That brings us to the next part. Point two: You will learn how to name an approval owner.

The measure this part speaks to is approval cycle time. Question for the chat: 'What did the last audit say about spend controls or approvals?'

Take one case from your own work and note where it stands on approval cycle time today.

One concern that comes up often: 'Our ERP already does this'. A fair way to settle it is to ask to see the gap between the ERP module and the daily workflow (approvals, receipts, cards, posting) using one month of your own transactions.

Next is point three, how to compare cycle time before and after one batch. Any questions before we move on? Put them in the chat."

### Main Content Block 3 (10 min)

**ON SCREEN: Key concept slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"Last, and the most practical part. Point three: You will learn how to compare cycle time before and after one batch.

The yardstick to keep in view here is approval cycle time. Question for the chat: 'Which part of this is hardest for your team?'

Before you change anything, write down where you stand today on approval cycle time, so there is a number to beat.

Another concern we hear: 'Security and compliance review'. A fair way to settle it is to prepare the answers before they are asked: data residency, access controls, audit logs, certifications you actually hold.

That covers the takeaways. Next, the summary. Any questions before we move on? Put them in the chat."

### Summary & Key Takeaways (4 min)

**ON SCREEN: Takeaways slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"To sum up, you have covered Count exceptions, how to name an approval owner and how to compare cycle time before and after one batch."

### Q&A (8 min)

**ON SCREEN: Q&A slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"Now your questions. I will read each one aloud from the chat and answer it.

If the chat is quiet, I will start with a concern we hear a lot: 'Migration will disrupt the close'. A fair way to settle it is to plan the cut over just after a month end close and run old and new in parallel for one cycle.

Questions we do not reach will be answered in the follow-up email."

### Close & CTA (2 min)

**ON SCREEN: Next step slide**

**SPEAKER:**
"If you do one thing this week, name an approval owner.

If you would like to take this further, reply to the follow-up email and ask for a conversation about the first step.

Thank you for joining."

**END WEBINAR**

---

## Q&A Preparation (for the host, not read aloud)

### Anticipated Questions

1. **"How do we get started with this?"**
   - Answer pattern: Deals in fintech, spend and expense usually start like this: CFO led with a security and compliance review inside the cycle; proof through a pilot on one entity or department.

2. **"Our ERP already does this"**
   - Answer pattern: Show the gap between the ERP module and the daily workflow (approvals, receipts, cards, posting) using one month of the buyer's own transactions.

3. **"Security and compliance review"**
   - Answer pattern: Prepare the answers before they are asked: data residency, access controls, audit logs, certifications you actually hold.

4. **"Migration will disrupt the close"**
   - Answer pattern: Plan the cut over just after a month end close and run old and new in parallel for one cycle.

5. **"Can you share more examples of this: Count exceptions?"**
   - Answer pattern: Use an example that follows this shape: close time or reconciliation effort before and after for one entity, signed off by the finance controller.

6. **"How does this compare to what we do today?"**
   - Answer pattern: Ask what their current setup does not do (reconciliation, month end close are good places to look), then show the difference on that point only.

---

## Follow-Up Sequence

### Email 1: Same day

**Subject:** Thank you for joining: Reduce invoice exceptions before the payment run

Thank you for joining.

The takeaways, in short:
1. Count exceptions
2. How to name an approval owner
3. How to compare cycle time before and after one batch

Questions? Reply to this email.

---

### Email 2: Day 3

**Subject:** A concern from the session: Regulatory caution

The concern we hear most is "Regulatory caution". A fair way to settle it is to map each requirement you name to the control or report that meets it; never claim a compliance status you cannot show.

---

### Email 3: Day 7

**Subject:** Your next step after the session

The natural next step is a conversation about the first step. Reply to this email if you would like it, or if you want to talk it through with Invoice processing service.

---

---

## Sector Notes: Fintech, spend and expense

- Readers in fintech, spend and expense are usually Chief Financial Officer, Finance Controller, Head of Accounts Payable. They watch days to close the books, reconciliation effort, policy breach rate, approval cycle time.
- **Who sits in the buying group:** The CFO signs; the Finance Controller or the head of the affected finance team champions; internal audit and compliance review controls; IT checks ERP integration and security; HR joins when employees are affected.
- **Terms this audience uses:** reconciliation, month end close, policy controls, audit trail, accounts payable, ERP posting.
- **Objections to expect:** our erp already does this; security and compliance review; migration will disrupt the close; regulatory caution.
